content: 1. A composition that has been intentionally altered through genetic engineering refers to a deliberate modification of an organism's genetic material, as opposed to changes occurring naturally or accidentally (Collin, 2001). 2. Ground release involves the release of sterile insects directly from the ground into the environment. 3. Impacts refer to the long-term effects or consequences of a particular action or intervention. 4. Implementation is the process of putting a plan or decision into effect, making it active or operational (Merriam-Webster). 5. Infective describes the ability of an organism, such as a pathogen or vector (e.g., mosquito), to cause infection (adapted from WHO, 2016). 6. Intervention is a deliberate action aimed at improving health by reducing the risk, duration, or severity of a health problem (Jamison et al., 2006). 7. Beneficial organisms are introduced with the expectation of achieving a rapid and positive effect (FAO, 2006). 8. The life cycle of an organism refers to the sequence of stages in its growth and development, ultimately leading to the reappearance of the initial stage (Whiteside et al., 1988; Hill, 1997). 9. A living modified organism (LMO) is any living organism that contains a novel combination of genetic material obtained through modern biotechnology (Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, 2000). 10. A living organism is any biological entity capable of transferring or replicating genetic material, including sterile organisms, viruses, and viroids (Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, 2000). 11. Local strain or local material refers to colonized mosquitoes derived from specimens collected in the general area targeted for the release of sterile males in a Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) program. The term general is subject to interpretation by regulatory bodies. 12. Longevity, also referred to as lifespan, is the length of life of an individual or a population (Hill, 1997). 13. Mark-release-recapture is a technique used to estimate insect population size by marking, releasing, and recapturing individuals, then calculating their proportional abundance (Daly et al., 1998). 14. Mass rearing is a systematic process conducted in integrated facilities using machinery to produce large numbers of insects for release. The goal is to produce acceptable insects at the lowest possible cost (Lepple et al., 1982; Singh, 1977). 15. Migration refers to the long-range dispersal of organisms, either away from a declining resource or as part of a seasonal cycle (Gordh and Headrick, 2001; Auburn, 2008). 16. Modern biotechnology involves the application of in vitro nucleic acid techniques, such as recombinant DNA and direct injection of nucleic acids into cells or organelles, or the fusion of cells beyond the taxonomic family. These techniques overcome natural reproductive or recombination barriers and are not used in traditional breeding and selection (Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, 2000). 17. Genetically modified mosquitoes (GMM) are mosquitoes whose genetic material has been altered in a way that does not occur naturally through mating or natural recombination (Directive 2001/18/EC). Irradiated mosquitoes, however, are not considered genetically modified organisms (GMOs) but are instead randomly mutated and excluded from GMO classification. 18. A mother colony is the original colony of insects established from field-collected specimens. The offspring of the mother colony are used to create other colonies, known as daughter colonies. The mother colony is maintained under conditions as similar as possible to field conditions (Parker, 2007; Franz, 2005). 19. Outcomes refer to the short-term effects or results of an intervention or action. 20. Oviposition is the act or process of laying eggs, involving the passage of an egg from the median oviduct to outside the insect's body (Resh and Cardé, 2003; Gordh and Headrick, 2001). 21. A population is a group of organisms of a single species that are potentially interbreeding and occupy a particular space at the same time (USDA, 1993; MCC, 1996; Wikipedia, 2008; Pedigo, 2002; Resh and Cardé, 2003). 22. Population elimination refers to the disappearance of an isolated population of vectors in a given area as part of a vector control strategy. This concept differs from species eradication (HCB, 2017). 23. Population modification is a vector control strategy aimed at reducing the ability of individual vectors in a population to transmit a specific pathogen, without necessarily altering the population size. This is distinct from population reduction strategies (HCB, 2017). 24. Population reduction is a vector control strategy designed to decrease the size of a vector population below the threshold required for pathogen transmission, without affecting the vector competence of the remaining individuals. This is distinct from population modification strategies (WHO, 2014; HCB, 2017). 25. Quality control is a systematic process in which management critically evaluates production elements, establishes standards and tolerances, collects and analyzes data on production and product performance, and provides feedback to predict and regulate product quality and quantity (FAO/IAEA/USDA, 2003). 26. Release refers to the intentional liberation of an organism into the environment (FAO, 2006). 27. The rolling carpet principle involves carrying out various operational phases of pest management simultaneously in a phased manner, with intervention progressing in a unidirectional front (Hendrichs et al., 2007). 28. A vector control technique is considered self-limiting if its effects are confined to a specific space and time unless the technique is continuously applied. For techniques involving the release of modified insects, the modification will disappear from the population unless reintroduced through regular releases (HCB, 2017). 29. A stakeholder is anyone with an interest, concern, or stake in an entity or its actions (Oxford Dictionary, 2008). 30. A sterile insect is one that does not produce viable offspring due to a specific treatment, rendering it unable to reproduce regardless of its mate (FAO, 2017). 31. The sterile-to-wild ratio, also known as the overflooding ratio, is the ratio of sterile insects to wild insects in a population within an SIT program (FAO/IAEA/USDA, 2003). 32. Suppression is a regulatory control program aimed at decreasing a target pest population within a geographical region. It involves reducing the pest population below a predetermined economic threshold (Gordh and Headrick, 2001; USDA, 1993). 33. Surveillance is an official process that collects and records data on pest occurrence or absence through surveys, monitoring, or other procedures. It involves detecting the presence of a pest species and determining its population density, dispersion, and dynamics (FAO, 2006; Pedigo, 2002; Gordh and Headrick, 2001). 34. The target population is the population of an organism that is the intended focus of an action or program. In the context of SIT, the target population is the wild population against which sterile insects are released (FAO/IAEA/USDA, 2003). 35. A vector (insect) is an organism capable of transmitting or transporting a microorganism, pathogen, or parasite from one host to another (Pedigo, 2002; Resh and Cardé, 2003; Gordh and Headrick, 2001). 36. Vectorial capacity (VC) is a measure of the intensity of pathogen transmission, calculated using the formula VC = ma² × pⁿ / log(p), where m = mosquito density per person, a = number of bites, p = daily survival rate of the mosquito, and n = duration (in days) required for the virus to amplify in the mosquito (extrinsic incubation period) (MacDonald, 1952). 37. The wave principle involves an expanding operational block size with each phase of an area-wide integrated pest management (AW-IPM) program using SIT (Hendrichs et al., 2007).
